appraisal_events.evidence: "j'ai failli le nommer... c'est épouvantable, heureusement que je me suis arrêtée à temps"; the duc adds "Vous n'avez qu'à dire qu'on remette ces dessins en haut, puisqu'ils vous font penser à Swann. Si vous ne pensez pas à Swann, vous ne parlerez pas de lui."
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann's very name has become something to be nervously avoided and managed in the Guermantes' conversation, treated with mock-alarm as an embarrassment rather than discussed as a person, which narratively erases and diminishes him in this elite circle.

appraisal_events.evidence: "l'envie qui lui avait fait feindre d'ignorer mon article cessait, comme un compresseur se soulève"; Bloch then remarks that it is humiliating to write "dans le journal du sabre et du goupillon, des five o'clock, sans oublier le bénitier."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly attributes Bloch's earlier silence to jealousy, and shows that once his own envy lifted, his belated comment on the narrator's article was really a disguised insult, exposing Bloch's professed delicacy as cover for petty envy.

status_effects.explanation: Swann is pointedly excluded from the conversation: his name must be avoided as embarrassing, reflecting his diminished, unspoken presence in this social circle.
Bloch's concealed jealousy and backhanded remark about the narrator's article expose him as petty and insincere, lowering how he comes across in this passage.

ambiguities: The taboo around naming Swann is voiced jointly by Mme de Guermantes and the duc; the source is attributed primarily to Mme de Guermantes though the duc's remark reinforces the same movement.
The closing paragraph, in which Mme de Forcheville reports Bergotte's admiration, is explicitly marked as a dream ('c'était un rêve'), so it is not treated as an actual appraisal event.
